amiberry-system-emulator.status: v8.4.2 remains the published baseline; development head now hard-resets stale 24/32-bit address-space transitions and adds bounded x86-64 JIT fault diagnostics
amiberry-system-emulator.notes: Identity: General-purpose UAE/WinUAE-derived Amiga system emulator. Current work continues post-v8.4.2 CPU, JIT and configuration correctness rather than creating a separate product. Classification: System emulation and debugging/runtime maintenance. Guest CPU-mode correctness does not change the distinction between Amiga m68k guests and modern host CPU families. Source CPU: m68k remains the emulated guest family. The reviewed change explicitly handles transitions between 24-bit and 32-bit guest address-space layouts. Target CPU: Existing documented ARM, x86, RISC-V and LoongArch64 host families remain unchanged. The new diagnostic path is specifically bounded to supported x86-64 JIT hosts and does not establish a new target. Build: Current head forces a hard reset when a CPU-mode change leaves the bank table laid out for the old 24/32-bit address space. It also logs bounded backtraces, memory-bank data and CPU state for x86-64 faults outside JIT code, guarded to libc platforms that provide backtrace support. Limitations: This is upstream source evidence on development head, not a new release or an independent emulator run. Runtime profiles: The change states no new host CPU, RAM or OS minimum. Existing published Windows/macOS ARM64/x86-64 variants and v8.4.2 Linux AppImage glibc 2.35 floor remain unchanged. AI: Existing scoped ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot evidence remains. The reviewed address-space commit contains no additional co-author attribution. Relationships: Amiberry remains a UAE/WinUAE-derived Amiga system emulator. External Kickstart ROMs, game media and third-party components retain separate provenance; the current CPU/JIT fix does not alter lineage. This GitHub repository is a readable preservation mirror, not asserted to be the original authors’ account. Classification: Original C plus substantial inline 68000 assembly, with actual game, editor, collision, terrain and drawing routines. Direct sound/screen-buffer access is original native Mac code. The source’s Mac II “emulation mode” means copying a software back buffer with QuickDraw, not interpreting a guest CPU. Source CPU: The authors expressly describe 68000 assembly, and Assembly Macros.h uses D/A registers, movea, adda and dbf. The historical 68000 branch and documented 68020-or-later Mac II rendering branch establish m68k without conflating host emulators with the game. Build: The assembly macros name Lightspeed C; the historical author account also discusses Megamax C. There is no pinned reproducible compiler/resource build, and the mirror’s latest commit explicitly adds only incomplete assets. Brian Wilson separately supplies the application, Continuum Galaxy data and full source archive. Limitations: No game compilation, dependency installation, launch, gameplay, hardware test or binary comparison was performed. Upstream claims remain separate from independently verified build flags. The complete original archive was not downloaded or compared to this mirror. Runtime profiles: Original documentation excludes 128K Macs and System 6.0 specifically on 512K-through-SE machines, while saying earlier/later systems work. On 68000 Macs the second graphics buffer conflicts with RAM cache, MacsBug and some INITs; the Mac II path allocates a buffer and uses CopyBits. These warnings are historical compatibility constraints, not advice to change the user’s system. AI: The inspected README, source/build files and up to twenty latest commit messages contain no affirmative development-AI attribution. This bounded negative search does not establish non-use; historic code dates and filenames are not treated as AI evidence. greaseweazle-rescue-floppy-workflow.notes: Identity: Greaseweazle Rescue is a substantive AutoIt Windows GUI and recovery-workflow layer over Greaseweazle. The current root contains v1.3.4 source and release notes, despite root README installation examples still naming v1.3.1. It handles PC/DOS/VGACopy, AmigaDOS ADF and C64/1541 D64 workflows. Classification: The source implements format detection, SCP capture, standard ADF/D64 conversion, direct retry reads, reports, hashes and conflict-safe publication of complete logical images. Its DOS path additionally implements targeted head-by-head adaptive rereads and multi-SCP sector merging. This is independent recovery automation around an existing decoder, rather than a claim to have reimplemented Greaseweazle's flux codecs. Limitations: The multi-SCP handler explicitly rejects Amiga and C64 modes. Advanced adaptive two-pass sector recovery is DOS-only; Amiga/C64 use direct Greaseweazle retry reads. Complete ADF/D64 standard sectors do not preserve all copy-protection or unusual flux data, so SCP remains the archival master. Source CPU: This tool reads floppy flux and disk-image sector data rather than reconstructing any original executable CPU instruction set. Supported disk platforms do not establish source CPUs. Target CPU: The AutoIt source, README and v1.3.4 release establish Windows as host, but no explicit x86/x64 target selection or minimum processor architecture was found. No architecture is inferred from AutoIt or Windows. Build: The repository supplies a substantial AutoIt source script and tagged v1.3.4 release, whose inspected release assets list is empty. Root README describes a compiled EXE but no such artifact was verified. No AutoIt compilation, hardware capture, recovery trial or independent image comparison was performed; all build flags remain unknown. Limitations: The 100_PERCENT_OK label means all expected standard sectors were reported present; it is not historical binary equivalence or completeness of copy-protected flux. Runtime profiles: The creator README explicitly requires Windows 7 or later, Greaseweazle gw.exe and compatible hardware/drive for physical capture. Record the documented OS requirement, leaving CPU/RAM unclaimed. AI: Inspected README, complete current root, source and both available commit messages include no explicit AI development attribution. The README's self-evaluation tone is not evidence of AI authorship. Relationships: The README explicitly credits and requires Keir Fraser's already-tracked Greaseweazle tools. This separate AutoIt implementation adds workflow, reporting and DOS-sector rescue logic and is not a mirrored copy of those tools. The root license is MIT. lanthorn-interactive-fiction-archive.notes: Runnable Rust terminal interpreter for Z-machine, Glulx and Scott Adams formats, with loaders for original ADF, ST, D64, DSK and other disk images, automapping and artwork rendering. v0.9.3 moves new installations to platform-standard data folders, adds a migration command and Glulx border defaults, and bounds runaway stories plus damaged media/image/audio handling. This is historical story/media format implementation, not a claim of recovered game source. v0.9.5 adds game-probed automap exits and non-cardinal room placement, Scott Adams autocomplete, and single-pass/lazy media reads that reduce a documented 354 MiB CD launch from repeated full-image reads to about 27 MiB. It also corrects narrower-window save restoration, multi-command mapping and platform data-folder migration. The following unreleased compass styling is not promoted into the release status. Evidence: https://github.com/sharkusk/lanthorn/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md https://github.com/sharkusk/lanthorn/releases/tag/v0.9.5 v0.9.6 publishes Linux x86-64/aarch64, macOS universal and Windows x86-64 archives. Current main prevents modal dialogs from being hidden under full-screen artwork by using terminal-protocol-specific fallback behavior for sixel/iTerm2 and Kitty graphics, and replaces fixed PTY test delays with content-based staging; the commit reports the affected test dropping from roughly 37 seconds to 2.5 seconds. These commits explicitly credit Claude Opus 5.5. A tooling emulator and partial OS-API reimplementation, not recovered source for the guest compilers. load_cpm68k reads the 0x601a executable header, creates a basepage and relocates text/data/BSS; trap 2 implements BDOS and trap 3 BIOS, with host fopen/fread-backed files. Trap 0 handles supported Linux-style services and trap 15 Fondse-style calls. The direct-run path constructs runtime state without booting CP/M or loading a ROM. 68000 is explicit in README, m68000.cxx and the loaders. CP/M-68K is retained under canonical CP/M; Linux here means the supported m68k ELF/syscall convention, not every Linux executable. README requires its newlib startup/BSP stubs for sample applications, and source explicitly limits BDOS to calls used by tested compiler families. Addresses are not constrained to physical 68000 24-bit behavior. Nested 6502/Z80/x86 interpreters running as guests do not expand m68 itself into those guest ISAs. MSVC and g++ release scripts compile the emulator; the Linux recipe links statically and the macOS recipe sets signed-char behavior. The nested 68000 build uses m68k-elf-gcc, explicit 68000 options and newlib BSP support. Guest cross-compiler construction is separate: README reports GCC 8.2 build difficulties on macOS/Pi 5 and a GCC13 guest-test issue. These are maintainer claims, not independent failures here. nd120-reconstructed-verilog-cpu.status: Reconstructed ND-120 Verilog system with measured Tang Nano boot profiles and physical MEGA65 R6 bring-up to OPCOM; fresh-clone Nexys DDR2 and nested MEGA65 submodule build gaps are also corrected, while R3 hardware and MEGA65 SINTRAN remain untested.
nd120-reconstructed-verilog-cpu.notes: Identity: A reconstruction of the 1988 Norsk Data ND-120 3202D CPU board from original design documents, first represented in Logisim and now maintained as Verilog. Includes CPU/decode gate arrays, PAL translations, microcode, MMU and bus devices, simulation harnesses and FPGA board integrations. This is a hardware/firmware reconstruction distinct from the catalogued nd100x and nd500x software emulators. Classification: Actual board-independent core and CPU/peripheral instantiation inspected. README claims SINTRAN III boots on Tang Nano, Nexys and MiSTer; MEGA65 bitstreams are timing-clean but not yet run on real MEGA65. Treat hardware claims as upstream reports. Root MIT licence inspected. Original 1988 design scans, firmware and other inherited material require their own provenance assessment. Source CPU: Reconstructed architecture is ND-120 from original schematics, PAL equations and microcode. Target CPU: Logical CPU in generated FPGA bitstream remains ND-120. FPGA vendor silicon and simulator C++ host are not claimed as native instruction-set output. Build: Primary documentation now reports physical MEGA65 R6 bring-up to OPCOM at 20 MHz with 4 MB configured main memory and a 640x480 console. Separate commits make the Nexys build synthesize its gitignored DDR2 IP checkpoint and initialize the MEGA65 framework's nested QNICE submodule in fresh clones. Limitations: The tracker did not synthesize or run these cores. R3 hardware is untested and SINTRAN has not yet been tried on the physical MEGA65 R6. Runtime profiles: The verified-profile set now includes physical MEGA65 R6 bring-up: a 20 MHz ND-120 configuration with 4 MB configured main memory boots to OPCOM on a tester's board. This is one evidenced configuration, not a minimum; R3 and full SINTRAN use remain unverified. AI: The MEGA65 hardware-status commit explicitly carries a Claude Fable 5.1 Co-Authored-By trailer, establishing bounded AI contribution evidence for this project. Relationships: Repository renamed from RonnyA/nd-120 to RetroCoreLabs/nd-120; both URLs screened. Distinct from ND100X and ND500X emulators. ntvdm-dos-cli-runner.status: Substantive source reviewed; independent build, runtime and equivalence untested
ntvdm-dos-cli-runner.notes: David Lee’s NT Virtual DOS Machine is an independent portable 8086/text-mode DOS runner, distinct from Microsoft’s system NTVDM component. ntvdm.cxx loads .COM and MZ/ZM .EXE files, applies relocations and runs i8086.cxx. README documents direct console/script use of MASM, Link, Microsoft C, Turbo Pascal/C, QuickBasic and other legacy tools. Original test software is included but does not become reconstructed source or separate runner records. Canonical root was absent from the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and the prior deduplication index. Inspected default-branch head: 0649657d912f23e60b32971d1c45653d48b440e3. Tooling combines an 8086 interpreter with partial DOS 3.00-style APIs, BIOS/text-console and selected interrupt behavior. The loader creates PSP/environment and synthetic interrupt stubs; DOS file calls use native host fopen/fread/fwrite and -r maps a host directory to C:. Original executables run without a booted DOS OS or vendor ROM in the normal path. Optional boot-sector loading does not establish a complete PC hardware emulator. The guest CPU is explicitly Intel 8086 and source_platforms=DOS; a compiler producing other target code does not change the executed guest ISA. README excludes graphics, sound and mouse and cautions that CPU/cycle fidelity is incomplete. It documents application-specific limitations such as QuickC incremental linker access to missing memory control blocks and a COBOL linker requiring 286. The 8086 capability must not be expanded to general 286/protected-mode compatibility. README explicitly lists Windows x64/ARM64, Linux x64/x32/ARM32/ARM64/RISC-V, and macOS ARM64 M1/M3. It also reports big-endian builds for 68000 via m68 and SPARC v8 via sparcos, which are emulated-runtime outputs rather than independent tests on physical legacy machines. Canonical x86, x86-64, ARM, ARM64, RISC-V and m68000 labels are retained. The pinned m68/ntvdm/mntvdm.sh recipe explicitly selects 68000 and builds ntvdm.elf using the newlib/BSP route; it assumes guest source files have been made available locally, and was not run. The SPARC-v8/Linux route through sparcos remains an explicit maintainer runtime claim in notes: no concrete ntvdm SPARC build/output recipe was identified, so SPARC is omitted from target_cpu. No cross-product guarantee across all hosts and CPUs is claimed. MSVC/g++ scripts build the C++ interpreter/runtime; Linux release links statically with OpenMP and macOS uses pthread/signed-char settings. mr.sh deliberately uses -O2 and documents a maintainer-observed g++11.4 -O3/-Ofast code-generation problem. The pinned-head Windows-2022 MSVC CI run succeeded and archived ntvdm.exe, but its workflow runs no guest regression suite. README and commit test reports remain upstream claims; no compiler, test harness or DOS guest was executed here. paratos.status: Substantive source reviewed; experimental compatibility; build and runtime independently untested
paratos.notes: ParaTos is an experimental direct runner for original Atari TOS/MiNT command-line applications. README identifies Linux and explains the system-call translation approach. gemdos/loader.c reads and endian-converts the PRG header, builds the basepage/environment, copies text/data, applies relocation fixups and appends ARGV data. paratos.c loads the named executable and enters the CPU engine directly, without an ST machine boot. A 2023 upstream commit explicitly added OSX support, and current Apple-specific executable-path and byte-order code remains present; this refines the earlier discovery’s Linux-only evidence without asserting that a modern macOS build was tested. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot 9d43e70bce3ed4f82ee43e35375994332fc2ac4b, non-truncated tree with 106 entries. Tooling with CPU-emulator and GEMDOS/API-reimplementation capabilities. ParaTos invokes Musashi to execute original 68k instructions and dispatches guest trap calls to native host implementations; gemdos/path.c converts TOS/MiNT filenames to POSIX paths, with case-insensitive and 8.3-name lookup. It accepts U: and rejects other drive-letter mappings in this snapshot. This is not a compiler translating the guest to host source and not an ST hardware emulator. README restricts the intended programs to clean command-line tools avoiding direct hardware and OS trap-vector patching. The implementation is incomplete, and minimal BIOS/AES/VDI paths do not establish a desktop compatibility environment. The historical binaries are 68k TOS/MiNT programs. README calls the bundled engine m68000, while current paratos.c explicitly chooses M68K_CPU_TYPE_68020 for execution and disassembly. source_cpu records the documented 68000 family entry point and the concrete 68020 guest engine rather than silently retaining the discovery’s m68000-only description. paratos.c states that the FPU is not emulated. The test cross-toolchain prefix m68k-atari-mintelf- produces guest .tos binaries; it is not evidence for the CPU of the Linux/macOS host. memory.c contains an explicit __x86_64__ host branch that reserves the 68020’s four-gigabyte address space; this supports recording x86-64 as an implemented host target, not a tested runtime minimum. The alternative branch reserves 512 MiB and is not an identified support matrix for every 32-bit or ARM host; no additional CPU is inferred from that fallback, C11, Clang or macOS. memory.i explicitly assumes host unaligned loads/stores. Source-level Apple portability exists, but Apple Silicon support is not verified and is not implied by target_platforms including macOS. CMakeLists.txt declares CMake 3.10, C11, bundled mushashi and gemdos subdirectories and a paratos executable. The original OSX-support commit adds Apple byte order and executable-path logic, with guarded host API differences, retained at the inspected tip. pop2-macintosh-static-recompilation.notes: Identity: This project analyzes and recompiles the 68k Macintosh Prince of Persia 2 executable into C++ and WebAssembly. README names the Mac build as 1995 while repository description says 1994; this discrepancy is retained without guessing a release year. Source and current target are separate. Classification: A static 68k-to-C++ translation with Macintosh Toolbox/QuickDraw/Resource/Sound shims over SDL2. CMake compiles generated segment sources; runtime maps guest addresses to compiled function pointers, recognizes fixed jump/sound trampolines and aborts on unimplemented instructions. A guest register/flat-memory model and low-memory globals are retained, but inspected paths contain no general opcode interpreter or Macintosh hardware/chip emulator. This is not a high-level rewritten game engine. Limitations: Unresolved computed jumps may be treated as returns; absence of an interpreter in these paths is a bounded source inspection, not a runtime proof of complete translation. Source CPU: README explicitly identifies 68k source binaries; generated functions express D/A registers, condition codes, memory accesses and A-line Toolbox traps, corroborating m68k source rather than PowerPC. No exact original 680x0 minimum is established. Target CPU: CMake has native C++20/SDL2 and explicit Emscripten WebAssembly paths. The native runtime uses glibc-style execinfo backtraces outside Emscripten, making Linux a source-level inferred route rather than a verified upstream support promise. WebAssembly is the explicit virtual output architecture; the native host ISA remains unspecified and is not inferred from 68k input. Build: Requires CMake 3.20+, C++20, SDL2 and extracted resource/data trees; unar and Python handle the owned original. Generated segment code is checked in, but the original resource forks and game data are required at runtime. README claims levels 1–14 and the final boss work; the ending cutscene remains intermittent. Source inspection also notes unmapped-jump return assumptions. Limitations: No game compilation, dependency installation, launch, gameplay, hardware test or binary comparison was performed. Upstream claims remain separate from independently verified build flags. Runtime profiles: The source supports an Emscripten browser build and a native SDL2 route inferred to suit Linux from glibc-style code. CMake’s 256 MB initial WebAssembly memory is a build setting, not a tested minimum. Neither an exact original 68k model/OS/RAM minimum nor a modern browser version floor was established. AI: The pinned development log explicitly says the web player uses a Claude Design shell. This is affirmative development-AI evidence for frontend presentation only; neither generic generated-code comments nor absent agent filenames prove how the game recompiler was authored. Relationships: A standalone game-specific implementation, distinct from sp00nznet/macrecomp. The repo states users bring legally owned data and provides a no-preload file-picker mode. No root license was found in the pinned tree; generated code is derived from the game, and neither repository visibility nor “engine only” establishes redistribution rights. Upstream self-hosting/deploy flows may bundle external data, so they were not run. riscose.notes: One riscose project family is tracked across its original SourceForge home, repo.or.cz lineage and the inspected hamishcoleman/riscose GitHub tree. The original site describes SWI-level execution of unmodified RISC OS applications without a RISC OS ROM. README demonstrates direct GNU grep invocation with host stdin and filenames. Current main.c and mem.c load an application image at guest address 0x8000 and execute it through arm_run_routine. Although README still says Absolute executables only, current code and man/riscose.1 also expose module and utility modes; this is evidence of implemented paths, not complete compatibility. The GitHub tip is 2023-10-25; a prior indexed repo.or.cz summary reported 2023-11-02, but its direct access was geographically blocked. That lineage is retained without pretending the GitHub tip is the newest commit anywhere in the family. Canonical repository and lineage aliases were screened against the fresh 1702-project baseline at ac4ea751fcdb273322cfdac18cd679b83f03a90f and prior dedup index; no existing counted project matched. Source snapshot ec85f120327ce37ecee8bbcb90f3111330bd5bae, non-truncated tree with 231 entries. Tooling: original ARM instruction execution combined with RISC OS SWI/SharedCLib reimplementation, focused on command-line software rather than a whole Archimedes machine. configure.ac selects ARMulator by default, sleeve as an alternate interpreter, or a separate native ARM backend. src/swi.c dispatches registered native handlers, and xosfile_load_stamped translates a RISC OS filename then uses host open/fstat/read. Guest instructions are interpreted for the default route; native SWI handling is not a translation of the guest binary. The optional same-ISA native backend remains a distinct execution design, not proof of general modern ARM compatibility. Runtime API coverage is partial, and unregistered SWIs return an error in the inspected tip. ARM is the explicit guest ISA in the man page, loader interface and ARMulator integration. It extracts/decrypts CODE and resources, invokes the macrecomp lifter and supplies a real loader/entry harness. It is independent from the already tracked fab48 reforged remake. Classification: build.sh generates C segments from the user’s game and links them with the pinned macrecomp submodule. That exact dependency uses compiled C function-pointer dispatch, register/flat-memory semantics and Toolbox/QuickDraw/SDL2 shims. Unmapped calls and unsupported instructions log/return rather than invoking an opcode interpreter; no emulated Macintosh chipset was found in these inspected paths. This is mechanical translation, not a high-level gameplay rewrite. Limitations: The pinned runtime advances low-memory Ticks once per lifted call, an approximate timing model rather than a hardware timer; unsupported paths log and return. Source-level eligibility does not establish faithful timing or playable game completion. Source CPU: The inspected extractor/build instructions explicitly process original 68000 CODE segments, and loader jump-table entries check 68k LoadSeg thunk opcodes. m68k is the source architecture only. Target CPU: The build invokes a host C11 compiler and SDL2 via pkg-config; README specifically documents Windows/MSYS2 setup. The generic POSIX script is not sufficient to promise every Unix host. No fixed output ISA or verified minimum CPU is stated, so native target_cpu remains empty. Build: Upstream reports compiled/linked output drawing real one-bit intro content, explicitly parked before the event loop and not playable. The build needs the exact macrecomp submodule, Python macresources/machfs/capstone, a C compiler and SDL2. Original disk, extracted resources and generated C are omitted and must be supplied/regenerated. Decryptor byte-exact claims concern a protection-analysis oracle, not complete game equivalence. Limitations: No game compilation, dependency installation, launch, gameplay, hardware test or binary comparison was performed. Upstream claims remain separate from independently verified build flags. Runtime profiles: No independently established runtime minimum. The source allocates a 32 MB virtual address array and displays a 512×342 monochrome framebuffer; these implementation choices do not establish host RAM requirements or historical system-version support. AI: The head render-loop/calling-convention commit explicitly credits Claude Opus 4.8 as co-author, with the same disclosure on preceding implementation commits. This supports AI-assisted code development, without estimating what fraction was AI-authored. Relationships: The toolkit is a dependency, counted separately as audit-only context in this game pass. This root is not a fork of fab48’s distinct browser remake; the inspected sources/build pipeline independently establish a different code lineage. MIT applies to the project’s original harness/tooling, while original game code/assets remain copyrighted and absent. stellar7-apple2-iolo-reconstruction.notes: Identity: README and artifact provenance pin the supplied stella7.dsk and original manual. This repository maintains all 35 logical file representations, source and editable assets. README explicitly preserves original ownership and disclaims any implied redistribution license. Classification: Address-preserving ca65 game reconstruction plus lossless JSON assets and exact disk generation. The optional model viewer is an inspection aid; gameplay output remains the original Apple II program rather than a game-specific emulation wrapper. Source CPU: The recovered TITLE.2 decoder selects 6502 and contains native A/X/Y and zero-page operations. Other program/overlay files are reconstructed ca65 code; the launcher is Applesoft BASIC. Target CPU: The configured source uses .setcpu "6502" and the Makefile/README produce native Apple II disk images; host Python and Canvas model viewing do not establish another CPU target. Build: Upstream verification reports passing 17 tests, all 35 payload hashes, exact-image identity and a fresh second build. Apple2ts tests cover startup, menu, briefing, controls and a fixture-driven level transition; independent MAME reaches gameplay input. Those author-reported checks are preserved as evidence only. All four build flags remain unknown because this review did not independently build, compare or run the output. Limitations: Not rerun here. Full seven-system completion, save/high-score persistence, audio and joystick fidelity remain untested; Ctrl-R self-destruct is unresolved. Exact mode preserves original DOS/reserved/slack data, not reconstructed OS source. Runtime profiles: Upstream tests an Apple II+ configuration in MAME and a separate Apple2ts scenario, but does not establish minimum CPU/RAM requirements. These tested configurations are documented without inferring a minimum profile. AI: Commit 60dadd0 explicitly attributes the recovery to "single turn disassembly by astra"; status notes refer to installed Codex skills. AI usage is evidenced, but no interface label is inferred from the model-name attribution, so tools stays empty. Relationships: Distinct from the already tracked Andy McFadden SourceGen project: that project covers the official/4am release with an early ROCK3 loader, whereas this supplied disk includes an added TITLE.2 and different payload layout. Inspected bootstrap.py/recover.py generate ca65 source directly from assets/raw binaries with their own control-flow renderer and no SourceGen import. The root is non-fork; no borrowed SourceGen source is credited. This supports an independent reconstruction, not a format-converted mirror. thames-isis-cli-runner.notes: Mark Ogden’s maintained Thames source explicitly derives from John Elliott’s Thames 0.1.1. Elliott’s official page identifies an ISIS-II runner for the tools used to build CP/M3, and the maintained loader/interpreter confirm direct original-binary execution. Count the original tarball and enhanced fork as one lineage under ogdenpm/thames-src. CP/M3 is the build product of example guest tools, not the OS API being emulated. Modern tooling executes linked ISIS-II Intel OMF images, often without file extensions. isis_load accepts module/start/data/end records, loads bytes and rejects unresolved relocation/external/library records. main creates synthetic MDS BIOS/ISIS trap stubs in RAM, loads the argv-selected tool and enters the interpreter. ISIS OPEN/CLOSE/READ/WRITE/SEEK/LOAD translate to host files through device mapping; the path needs original tools/support files but no original boot ROM or booted ISIS OS. ISIS-II 8080/8085 binaries are the intended guest source. Ian Collier’s xz80 engine was reduced to 8080/8085 semantics by default; thames.h leaves Z80 disabled and documents an optional build switch. The VS Release|x64 project sets Z80 for thames.c only, not the z80.c interpreter unit; this is a configuration caveat, not evidence of universal Z80 compatibility. Source_cpu therefore records 8080 and 8085, preserving optional Z80 ancestry in notes. The Visual Studio project explicitly has Win32 and x64 configurations and MachineX86 for Win32, supporting host x86 and x86-64 labels. Windows/Linux device paths and Unix usage are explicit in documentation. The CMake route is portable C but provides no further CPU guarantee. macOS is not asserted merely from Unix/CMake portability; guest 8080/8085 and code emitted by ASM48/ASM51/PLM80 are not host architectures. CMake >=3.5 builds the C sources and runs Perl Scripts/getVersion.pl to generate version headers; a checked-in VS solution/project is the alternative. Unix line endings matter to the version generator’s dirty-tree detection. The complete tree contains no GitHub Actions workflow. Documentation’s successful guest-tool lists are maintainer reports, not current-host build proof, and the per-file VS Z80 define needs review if enabling the optional mode. No build or guest test was attempted. All four build flags remain null: compilation, execution, gameplay and byte-equivalence are independently unverified. Partial ISIS.LAB/ISIS.DIR synthesis, less-tested CONSOLE/WHOCON/line-mode I/O, Enter-dependent keyboard handling and heuristic tool-error detection materially limit compatibility. John Elliott origin and Mark Ogden enhancements remain one Thames family. The interpreter has GPL-2.0-or-later headers and COPYING is GPLv2; several ISIS/loader files have GNU Library GPL v2-or-later notices, so preserve mixed component terms. Original Intel tools are separately licensed. Documentation recommends newer native-C ports for several tools; those execute recompiled source and must not be conflated with Thames running originals. The latest commit imports a recovered validity_check chunk as validity_check_original but explicitly says it is not used yet. The current parser remains a separate replacement. The active validity_check can emit UNHANDLED COMMAND GIVEN; the recovered validity_check_original is not the active implementation. A net-worth FIXME is also retained. These defects prevent any claim of complete restored gameplay. All four build flags remain null: neither a recipe, a large source file nor the recovered historical fragment verifies compilation, runtime, playability or binary identity. One record covers the lost-file recovery, original C preservation and SDL adaptation, rather than counting each as a new game. The latest commit attributes a recovered validity_check fragment to Crashdisk's EAB post and preserves its incomplete/unused status; README links the broader Amiga recovery discussion. The original Odyssey 2/C64 ancestry is context, not a separately inspected code lineage in this batch. No root project-level LICENSE/COPYING grant was found in the complete tree or reviewed README. Original shipment with C source is not itself a modern redistribution grant; rights remain unresolved, and no unrestricted redistribution conclusion is recorded. volamos-amiga-cli-runtime.status: v0.11 published; sanitizer tracks exec.library allocation lifetime and catches guest use-after-free
volamos-amiga-cli-runtime.notes: Wine-style host runtime for classic AmigaOS m68k command-line tools: interprets guest instructions (optional m68k-crate trace JIT) and reimplements OS library calls in Rust. No Kickstart ROM is needed for normal use. It is generic development/analysis tooling, not a native reconstruction of a specific game; graphics, custom chips, Workbench GUI and games are explicitly out of scope. Linux/macOS build and guest execution are corroborated by current CI logs; published Windows x86-64 binaries compile but Windows/Wine runtime remains unverified. Interpreter/JIT parity covers six fixtures; comparison with vamos includes three documented known divergences, so it is not universal compatibility proof. The math-library shims now return comparison/test results in both D0 and 68k condition codes, matching the documented ROM calling behavior needed by SAS/C's scmieee.lib; before the fix, SAS/C double comparisons appeared equal and exp() overflow checks returned HUGE_VAL. Evidence: https://github.com/sidick/volamos/commit/de321627fd5f1c16ca6cc76020222d7f3c18d564 exec.library SetFunction now installs executable guest JMP entries, returns a synthesized callable stub for the previous host-backed handler, supports hook chaining and restoration, and is covered by an end-to-end guest test. The patch is deliberately limited to one guest invocation and does not emulate AmigaOS-wide persistent hooks. Evidence: https://github.com/sidick/volamos/commit/018fd8f047d27fa3f85948b1595f44acf3f6f596 v0.10 incorporates non-AUTOINIT disk-library loading and the MakeLibrary/AddLibrary/InitStruct/MakeFunctions exec paths. Current main also adds opt-in CLI handling for UAE's formatted debug port at $BFFF00 and Emu68's byte debug port at $DEADBEEF, routing guest diagnostics to stderr without claiming broader GUI/custom-chip emulation. Evidence: https://github.com/sidick/volamos/releases/tag/v0.10 https://github.com/sidick/volamos/commit/2ee28f5f2759a9ea5096ba7f0068c4ec4cf94011 https://github.com/sidick/volamos/commit/359f762476c061b3b487cdcaf1dc86acdc786dd9 https://github.com/sidick/volamos/commit/fcec136d6f7f416b89af11d6bb76f6c89c96a8f5 v0.11 publishes aarch64 Apple/Linux and x86-64 Windows/Linux archives. Current sanitizer work extends exec.library Allocate/Deallocate handling: allocations become uninitialized, frees become unaddressable/freed, and live MemChunk headers remain addressable to avoid false positives. It can catch guest use-after-free and optionally uninitialized reads, but deliberately has no redzones, so one-byte overruns remain outside the stated coverage. Upstream reports 1,109 workspace tests passing; real gcc/sc binary checks were not run and trap-level end-to-end tests substitute. The implementation commit explicitly credits Claude Sonnet 5. Tracked as adjacent tooling rather than as a source-reconstruction target. Current main adds an opt-in, unauthenticated loopback GDB remote server shared by Windows and Unix builds. The ED FE trap routes BDOS/BIOS calls to native C; CPMREDIR maps CP/M drives and FCB operations onto host files. Required bios.bin is the bundled tiny ZXCC-specific synthetic BIOS/BDOS shim, with Z80/bios.zsm source, not an original vendor ROM or full CP/M OS. Limitations: The figures and per-function equivalence are upstream results. The tracker did not execute the tests or boot a reconstructed game, and 35 checked-with-errors functions plus 22 drawn-with-errors functions remain.
